references.text: Job describes the wicked as spending their days in prosperity – a parallel to the rich man's good life on earth. See Job 21:13.

Jesus pronounces a 'woe' upon the rich, for they have already received their comfort – the same principle Abraham states regarding the rich man: he received his good things in his earthly life. See Luke 6:24.
The context of the parable: the rich man lived in luxury while Lazarus lay poor and sick at his gate. Abraham points back to this contrast. See Luke 16:19-21.
Those who have gone through suffering will now be comforted – Lazarus, who suffered evil in life, is now being comforted (παρακαλεῖται). See Revelation 7:16-17.
Blessed are you who weep now, for you shall laugh – a direct parallel to Lazarus's reversal of fortune from suffering to comfort. See Luke 6:21.
'Woe to you who are full now, for you shall hunger' – Abraham's words to the rich man reflect this principle of reversal. See Luke 6:25.
The Lord contrasts the joy of his servants with the pain of the wicked – an Old Testament parallel to the reversal between the rich man and Lazarus. See Isaiah 65:13-14.
The psalmist describes people who receive their portion in this life and are filled with earthly prosperity – something that recalls the fate of the rich man. See Psalm 17:14.
Paul has learned to be content in all circumstances – a contrast to the one-sided good life of the rich man and the one-sided difficult life of Lazarus. See Philippians 4:11-12.
Paul speaks of how suffering now leads to comfort (παράκλησις), the same Greek term used for Lazarus's comfort. See 2 Corinthians 1:5-7.
